extracted.intended_audience: educated public, students of natural history, and comparative anatomists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for assessing anatomical observations, comparative-brain claims, and evolutionary hypotheses — emphasizing observational rigor, representative evidence, literature fidelity, and the evidential requirements for accepting physical causes such as natural selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis must account for all phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: “A true physical cause is, however, admitted to be such only on one condition--that it shall account for all the phenomena which come within the range of its operation. If it is inconsistent with any one phenomenon, it must be rejected; if it fails to explain any one phenomenon, it is so far weak, so far to be suspected; though it may have a perfect right to claim provisional acceptance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a strict evaluative standard for physical hypotheses: test for internal consistency with known phenomena. Any inconsistency weakens or refutes the hypothesis; failure to explain a phenomenon reduces its strength. Treat acceptance as provisional where explanatory gaps remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional acceptance pending crucial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “I adopt Mr. Darwin's hypothesis, therefore, subject to the production of proof that physiological species may be produced by selective breeding... just as the chemist adopts the atomic theory, subject to the proof of the existence of atoms; and for exactly the same reasons...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept influential hypotheses provisionally when they have strong prima facie probability and unify facts, but demand missing critical evidence (here: proof that selective breeding can produce physiological species differing in fertility) before full acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require multiple converging lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “if admitted, the facts of Development, of Comparative Anatomy, of Geographical Distribution, and of Palaeontology, become connected together, and exhibit a meaning such as they never possessed before;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evolutionary explanations by their ability to bring together and explain results from development, comparative anatomy, biogeography, and paleontology. The convergence of independent fields strengthens a hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational rigor in anatomical claims (avoid distorted specimens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings that extracted brains lose shape and that a careless observer may mistake the uncovered condition of the cerebellum of an extracted and distorted brain for the natural relations of the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base anatomical conclusions on distorted or extracted specimens without verifying their in-situ relations; instead use skull casts, sections, and comparisons that preserve natural spatial relationships. Always check whether preparation artifacts could explain apparent differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cranial casts and internal skull features as reliable proxies
rubrics_metrics.description: “inasmuch as the brain in all mammals completely fills the cranial cavity, it is obvious that a cast of the interior of the skull will reproduce the general form of the brain... a cast of the cerebral chamber, representing the cerebrum of the ape, as completely covers over and overlaps the cast of the cerebellar chamber... as it does in the man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When brains cannot be examined in situ, use plaster casts of the cranial cavity and observable cranial grooves (e.g., for the tentorium or lateral sinus) to infer relative brain-part proportions and relations confidently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures must be from representative, undistorted specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that an inadequate or altered figure was taken as a typical representation of the Chimpanzee's brain and that such misrepresentations are greatly to be regretted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure illustrations and figures come from representative, well-preserved specimens; avoid generalizing from anomalous or 'profondement affaisse' (deeply collapsed/altered) examples. Reproducible, accurate figures are essential to valid claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful review and citation of prior authoritative work
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusation that Professor Owen either overlooked or 'unjustifiably suppressing' well-known facts from earlier anatomists (Tiedemann, Cuvier, Schroeder van der Kolk, Vrolik, Gratiolet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before asserting novelty or uniqueness, survey and acknowledge existing literature and prior figures; do not ignore or suppress prior contradictory evidence. Scholarly claims should engage with and explain earlier findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be an advocate who smooths over difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: “The last position in which I wish to find myself is that of an advocate for Mr. Darwin's, or any other views--if by an advocate is meant one whose business it is to smooth over real difficulties, and to persuade where he cannot convince.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific exposition, be candid about difficulties and unresolved issues rather than rhetorically eliminating objections. Honest exposition strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic/rank decisions should rest on multiple anatomical characters
rubrics_metrics.description: “his Family distinction resting chiefly on his dentition, his pelvis, and his lower limbs.” (i.e., human Family distinction is justified chiefly by non-cerebral characters.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning systematic rank (family, order, etc.), base decisions on a suite of consistent anatomical characters rather than a single organ system (e.g., brain alone). Consider relative systematic value of multiple traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess magnitude of structural differences without exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat: while structural differences between Man and apes are 'great and significant', it is 'equally wrong and absurd to exaggerate its magnitude' — differences between ape taxa may be as large or larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate differences quantitatively and comparatively across taxa, avoiding rhetoric that inflates gaps. Place human–ape differences in context of differences among other related groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on careful investigations by skilled anatomists
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'abundant and trustworthy evidence (consisting of the results of careful investigations directed to the determination of these very questions, by skilled anatomists)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to reproducible studies performed by competent investigators; look for replication and consensus among specialists when judging anatomical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential requirement for selection as full cause: fertility/sterility outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: “so long as all the animals and plants certainly produced by selective breeding from a common stock are fertile, and their progeny are fertile with one another, that link will be wanting. For, so long, selective breeding will not be proved to be competent to do all that is required of it to produce natural species.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accept selection as a sufficient cause of species formation, demonstrate that selection can produce forms that correspond to natural (physiological) species distinctions — notably patterns of fertility/sterility among crosses and hybrids.
